source.title: One Filters All: A Generalist Filter for State Estimation
source.authors: Shi-Qing Liu; Wen-Han Cao; Chang Liu; Ze-Yu He; Tianyi Zhang; Yi-Nuo Wang; S. Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines model-size scaling in state estimation, a different application setting and metric from language-model pretraining loss; it reports RMSE outcomes across pretrained backbones.
record.gate_note: The paper compares state-estimation RMSE across pretrained LLM backbones and reports per-system and average results in Table 10. These results bear on downstream performance versus scale (V6), but the study does not fit or test a power law for held-out language-model loss. Other RMSE results, including fine-tuning comparisons and non-LLM architecture ablations, do not test the listed versions. Figure 7 reports a scaling/efficiency plot, but its results are not needed in addition to Table 10 for the downstream performance comparison.
record.test_reason: The study swaps frozen pretrained LLM backbones of four sizes (124M to 13B) into its state-estimation filter and reports RMSE per system (Table 10). That is a downstream-performance-versus-scale result in a new setting, bearing on V6. It fits no power law and does not relate performance to pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim scaling-law behaviour: average RMSE decreases as backbone size grows, at the cost of longer training time per iteration. Two qualifiers belong in the paraphrase: the backbones are frozen and only the embedding and projection layers are trained, and in-context prompting was disabled for this comparison.
record.recipe_differences: Uses state-estimation RMSE across pretrained backbones rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy, token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal allocation. The size comparison uses different model families as well as sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Per-system outcomes differ across backbone sizes; OPT-1.3B is worse than GPT-2 on Selkov and Oscillator, and LLaMA-7B is worse than OPT-1.3B on three systems.
record.code_released: not stated; the paper says complete code will be released after organization and conflict-of-interest review.
record.problems: The scaling comparison covers four backbones from different model families, not a controlled size sweep within one family. The reported scale results use state-estimation RMSE, with no fitted power law or test of prediction from smaller runs; uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: None of the Table 10 RMSE-by-system or average results were left out. Figure 7 scaling/efficiency plot values were not separately extracted because Table 10 provides the reported RMSE comparisons; no version concerns runtime.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss; a fitted or predictive law (no curve is fitted and no larger run is predicted); a within-family size sweep (the backbones come from different families).
Whether a power-law form holds for frozen-backbone transfer; no fit is made.

record.verdict_notes: The LLaMA-7B values in Table 10 match the LLM-Filter-O column of Table 1 (no SaP prompt). The scale comparison mixes GPT-2, OPT and LLaMA families, so pretraining data and architecture vary along with size. There are only four points, no uncertainty and no fit. Figure 7's training-time results bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and bottleneck conditions.
Whether fits on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Depth, width, and other architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes. The study reports an RMSE trend with backbone size, but does not test a power-law form.
The study tests state-estimation performance across pretrained backbone sizes, but does not relate it to pretraining loss or establish a fitted predictive relationship.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and bending of curves away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Average RMSE across the five systems, frozen backbones, no in-context prompt
relationships.reason: Average RMSE falls monotonically with backbone size: 0.9819, 0.9182, 0.7694, 0.6882 (r6, r12, r18, r24). This is a trend, not a fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: Average RMSE decreased monotonically with backbone size from 0.9819 through 0.9182 and 0.7694 to 0.6882, without a fitted scaling law.

relationships.condition: Per-system results, especially Lorenz96, VL20 and Selkov/Oscillator at 1.3B
relationships.reason: Improvement is non-monotonic per system. OPT-1.3B is worse than GPT-2 on Selkov and Oscillator (r7, r8). Lorenz96 is flat across all sizes (r4, r10, r16, r22). LLaMA-13B is worse than OPT-1.3B on VL20 (r11, r23). Model family is confounded with size.
relationships.display_finding: Lorenz96 performance stayed flat, OPT-1.3B underperformed GPT-2 on Selkov and Oscillator, and LLaMA-13B trailed OPT-1.3B on VL20, with family confounding size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Average RMSE across the five tested systems for GPT-2, OPT-1.3B, LLaMA-7B, and LLaMA-13B
reader_labels.reason: The reported average RMSE declines across the four backbone sizes, from 0.9819 to 0.6882 (r6, r12, r18, r24). This is a scale-related trend, not a fitted predictive law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: System-specific comparisons, especially GPT-2 to OPT-1.3B and OPT-1.3B to LLaMA-7B
reader_labels.reason: RMSE does not improve monotonically at every tested size transition: OPT-1.3B is worse than GPT-2 on Selkov and Oscillator, and LLaMA-7B is worse than OPT-1.3B on Hopf, Lorenz96, and VL20 (r1-r5, r7-r11, r13-r17).
